text:
The struggle of discomfort in games

There's one thing games seem to struggle with - conveying friction and discomfort. Now, you might argue that there's a lot of games rife with friction, as well as games that feel discomforting, but I think it's always done in sort of roundabout way. Let me explain. In real life when going somewhere we usually walk. We can run and we can sprint, which gets us to our desired destination faster, but even if it would have no negative consequences (sweat, danger of falling, social awkwardness) people will rather just walk. In video games we're almost always going as fast as we can. Games can have audio-visual cues and indicators that make the player feel like the character doesn't want to run (anymore), they can have various limitations and mechanics that prevent running all the time, but players are almost always maximizing their speed within these restrictions. It seems like the biggest insult to players is when they have to follow or be followed by a NPC who doesn't match their maximum speed. The only thing that makes me stop holding that sprint button is physical discomfort from holding it down for extended periods of time, which is quite funny. Of course movement is just one example. Carrying things is another great example. Again, there are often mechanics that limit or reward the player in one way or another, but players will just optimize within those restrictions. If I have inventory space and I'm not hitting some weight threshold then I am going to pick up a random bauble, whereas I definitely wouldn't do that same IRL - picking up junk we don't need is just not what we do. However this isn't just about negative experiences and discomfort, but about the opposite as well. People deeply enjoy eating good meals, but in games the only difference between hardtack and lavish feast is just some points in a mechanic that people optimize away. Relationships and especially intimate situations are another thing that games fail spectacularly at, but that's for a different discussion. I think expressing comfort and discomfort is one of the biggest blind spots in games. The problem is that in order to incentivize player to behave in a specific way, you kind of have to add more complex mechanics, perhaps layer interacting mechanics on top of each other. That dramatically increases the game's complexity and the ruleset can quickly become too complex or overwhelming. And you can't just hide mechanics because players come with expectations from other games. However I don't think it's impossible. Some games have successfully baked (dis)comfort into their core gameplay loop. A great example is how Factorio leverages player's discomfort, specifically boredom into action and progression. It is possible to spend hundreds of hours mining and crafting everything required to unlock and build the rocket, which is the game's win condition, but it would be incredibly dull and boring. It's natural human instinct to want it to speed up, and players just find a pace that suites them, they instinctively know how fast is fast enough. They don't need to be told, there don't need to be any systems pushing them towards it. However games such as Factorio focus on a very specific kind of discomfort. I have yet to see a game that does something similar with more broader range of situations and applications, for example an RPG. One thing I'm sure about is that if a game manages it, it will be greatly successful.
label: game_design

text:
DLSS 5 - A discussion

With DLSS 5 being pretty controversial, it's tough to have a genuine discussion about it, so I thought it may be a good idea to try it here. I was initially sceptical, but curious about DLSS 5. With the performance hits, I was hoping to at the very least use it on older games, similarly to RTX Remix. Unfortunately, that isn't really gonna happen. Out of my own testing and things I have seen others do, here are the main points I have of this technology so far: 1) It doesn't like old or abstract graphics My hopes about using it for older games were destroyed when in most older games it did.....nothing. Or almost nothing. In anything before last PS3 era, it likely won't "detect" anything that it knows what to do it, and thus won't do much. At best it may detect a face......but that is sadly often not a good thing. 2) Faces.....oh no The faces are very consistently at the bottom of the uncanny valley. It is definitely the main point of DLSS 5, and also the most controversial, divisive, and arguably the worst point. I've seen very few cherry picked examples of a face not looking extremely uncanny. It's especially bad when it does a lot of work on the face, but barely any on the rest of the body, making the face even more detached visually from the rest. This is the main reason why if someone would want to use this, I would highly avoid any game with a lot of faces, and think it would be a lot better if there was an option to disable faces entirely. 3) Gun models, vehicles and cockpit views This is likely where DLSS 5 is the best at. While the result often look overly similar, especially in terms of the material sheen, the general shading is usually pretty good. Due to them often being in the same position on screen for longer periods of time, it makes them more consistent too. However, I did notice in certain racing games that the lighting and shading can freak out in cases where the outside lighting changes abruptly (driving under trees for example), which leads us onto.... 4) Temporal stability....or rather lack there of Maybe this will be better with "official" implementations of it, but all the showcases of it that I've seen so far seemed to have been purely screen-based. This means it works just like ReShade, working purely off of the things that are currently visible on screen. This means that walking through a corridor, the light off screen may change from looking like sunlight, to flashlight, to room light, in a span of a few seconds, so even if the lighting in shading generally looks nice, you will keep getting distracted by it changing randomly. It also means that if some elements are frequently not visible, then the way they look will keep being very unstable. This is especially bad in some older games where it does detect a player model, but only from the front, so if it's a game where the player model keeps changing direction relatively to the camera, the way the player looks will keep changing all the time as DLSS 5 will either do different things to it, or will not know what to do at all when it doesn't see the front. This all leads to the final point and my main issue with this technology: 5) It's all just guessing Unlike RTX Remix, which actually takes all the data from the game engine directly, meaning that it's aware of all the geometry, lighting, materials etc, DLSS 5 is literally guessing what it's seeing and what to do with it. This inherently will be problematic in any game that isn't almost completely static, as it very much will be guessing wrong frequently, and even in the good cases it is noticeable if you actually play it for more than 3 minutes. This is essentially on similar level as hallucinated videos, or messed up AI movie upscales. The issue isn't that it's wrong or looks bad, but that it may look wrong or bad the moment you move the camera the wrong way. But those are just my thoughts on this, based on my own testing and things I've seen. I am curious what your experience with it was so far and what you think of it.
label: gaming_culture

text:
As my tolerance for friction fades, I’m finding "game feel" and immediacy matter more than systems depth. Is there a term for this design philosophy?

I've been in a weird gaming rut and trying to figure out the common thread in what actually works for me right now. Some context: my favorite games ever include Monster Hunter World, Dark Souls, Elden Ring, Breath of the Wild, Outer Wilds, Dyson Sphere Program, Minecraft, etc. I have no problem with depth or complexity. I love getting lost in big systems-heavy games. But lately the thought of booting up Monster Hunter and re-learning all those menus and loadouts, or opening Skyrim and dealing with my mod list, just feels exhausting. What's been working instead are boomer shooters on easy mode. They're all killer no filler. You just move and shoot. No skill trees, no crafting, no battle pass, no tutorial that treats you like you've never held a controller. I've tried roguelikes too since they seem like an obvious answer for "jump in and play" games. Hades, Dead Cells, Slay the Spire, Risk of Rain 2. Never liked any of them. I think the whole procedural generation thing and the feeling of "failing" runs creates its own kind of friction that I bounce off of. The authored, handcrafted experience might actually be a big part of what I'm after, I hadn't really thought about it until now. So I guess my question is: is there a name for this design philosophy? Games where the core interaction is so good that that's basically the whole game, and you're invited to just perform the action rather than manage all the stuff around it? Boomer shooters are the obvious example but I feel like it shows up elsewhere too. Arcade racers, beat em ups, 3D platformers maybe. Do other people feel this pull away from systems toward pure "verbs"? Is there a term for it that I'm just not aware of? And what other genres or scenes are actually making games like this right now?

text:
Games that require you to own/play the previous installment

Dunno if any such games exist, but I've been seeing a bunch of streamers play Mass Effect recently and it awakened some of my annoyances with the franchises original trilogy, and I wanted to talk about them. I appreciate that, conceptually, locking content and especially endings behind owning other games / buying other products, that it would annoy some people. Yet, if you are doing a narrative focused game where each instalment is an immediate followup of the previous in terms of story, where you take everything I do in one game and use that to decide what the state of the sequel is, all while implying my decisions matter? I feel like it's only fair that, as someone that puts a lot of time and effort into one game, investing heavily into the story, mechanics and emotionally? You reward that by giving me something. Mass Effect 1 had these resources. Half you get by scanning planets, the other half you get by exploring planets in the most scuffed vehicle I've ever had to use. It was a nightmare. But here's the thing. You cannot do ANYTHING with those resources. They sit in storage, and await Mass Effect 2, because that is the game where you will use them. And so, I spent time getting every resource I possibly could, only to reach ME2 and find out it did not matter. Because ME2 gives you all the resources you need. The only benefit to doing those minigames in ME1, is so you don't have to do a better optimised version of that minigame in ME2. Yeah, a better and more optimised version. Literally no reason to do it in ME1, unless you were under the impression it would have an actual use. Or what about story implications. Mordin have a big amazing questline in ME3? Well, hopefully you didn't let him die in ME2, which companions can die if you don't perfect it. Mordin? He has a 50% chance to die if you perfect ME2. I had to save scum THREE TIMES at the end of the game before I finally got an ending where he didn't randomly die. To anyone that did let him die? Well shucks, guess you will experience that exact same questline, in the exact same way, with a random ass background character who appeared out of nowhere. The only difference is some of the dialogue, but literally everything else is the same. "Had to be me, someone else might've gotten it wrong" he says. Fuck that's not true. Literally someone else will do it if he dies and you decide to live with it. While some of the characters have arguable variations if you let them die, where someone else does their thing but they have a different personality, so sometimes you get some lore implications. But in terms of what quests are available, nothing changes. No content is denied to you if you let someone die, or you didn't play the other games. I know other people think the emotional / lore side is enough, but I was just so disappointed being told my choices matter and it just never felt like it did. I save these characters and it felt like there was little to no impact on the world or story. I personally would've loved if ME3 (The ending was shit imo) had a "Perfect" ending that was only achievable to those of us that had been with the franchise from the beginning and got perfect endings in each previous instalment. Narrative focused games with continuous story instalments are the only games where I have this opinion on, so not many games would've met that for me. But sometimes it feels like playing multiple games in this scenario entitles you to a couple references, jokes or a nostalgia mission and nothing else.
label: game_design

text:
Deep Combat Mechanics But Without Any Reason To Use Them

I love games that actually try to be games rather than interactive movies. Games that put a strong emphasis on gameplay, whether that means deep combat, exploration, or other mechanics that give the player interesting ways to interact with the game world. Recently, I was playing Bright Memory: Infinite, and I found myself thinking about something that I see in a lot of games: having complex combat mechanics doesn't necessarily mean having deep combat. Bright Memory: Infinite gives you a surprising number of tools to use in combat. Your sword can attack, block, and parry, while your character can also dodge. You have offensive abilities through the sword and mechanical arm, firearms with primary and secondary attacks, different variations for each weapon, and even stealth in certain sections. On top of that, there are upgrades that further enhance these mechanics. On paper, this sounds like a lot of depth. The game gives you plenty of things to learn and plenty of tools to experiment with. But then I started asking myself: why should I actually use most of them? I kept finding myself doing the same things over and over because I never felt particularly motivated to use the other mechanics. Not necessarily because they were bad, but because the game rarely gave me a reason to engage with them. Take the parry, for example. Why would I spend time learning the timing of a parry when I can simply dodge the attack instead? Dodging is safer, easier, and more consistent. It also gives me an opportunity to reposition myself and continue attacking from a safer distance. Unless the game creates situations where parrying provides a meaningful advantage, learning the mechanic starts to feel like an unnecessary investment. And I think that's the bigger problem I'm trying to describe. There's a difference between giving the player more options and giving the player meaningful reasons to use those options. A combat system can have blocking, parrying, dodging, multiple weapons, secondary attacks, abilities, upgrades, and stealth, but if one or two approaches are consistently safer, easier, or more effective, then most of those mechanics become things that exist rather than things that matter. For me, good combat design isn't necessarily about how many mechanics a game gives you. It's about how the game encourages you to understand those mechanics and, more importantly, makes you want to use them. I would rather have five mechanics that constantly interact with each other and force me to make meaningful decisions than fifteen mechanics that I can mostly ignore without being meaningfully punished for it. So I'm curious what other people think: when does a combat system actually become "deep"? Is it simply the number of mechanics and options available to the player, or does there need to be some kind of encounter design, enemy design, resource system, or other incentive that makes those mechanics necessary or desirable to use? in other words... well, what is ya opinion?
label: game_design

text:
Vintage Story: why I think that there should be more processing-focused crafting systems

When I think of a crafting system, I think of collecting a number of reagents and throwing them into a grid. Usually the bottleneck is collecting many assorted items that I honestly don't keep track of. Then, the payoff is clicking "craft" in a menu and receiving my item. Then I discovered Vintage Story, which is like Minecraft if it slowed down and fleshed out all of its mechanics. The two strongest metals in the game are iron and steel. Both of these come from the same ore [iron], which is why I was shocked that the game gave me a massive vein of it that took three trips to empty. As it turns out, getting iron is easy, but processing it is hard. The first thing is that your standard crucible can't get hot enough to smelt it, so you need to make bloomeries and coal. Those both have their own processes, but the point is that your smelted iron has slag on it. You need to hit it with a hammer to knock off the slag and shape your ingots. There are more advanced recipes that let you use iron ingots, but it's much better to preprocess them into iron plates. You can semi-automate both of these things with a windmill or waterwheel attached to a helve hammer, which still needs help from you. Steel requires processing the iron ingots using a particular setup and lots of attention/fuel over multiple in-game days. It takes a lot of time, but it's a nice project during the in-game winter where you can forge while it snows outside. My point is, literally getting the materials for these items is easy, but it takes a lot of work to process it. I rarely see this in games and it was a refreshing perspective that really made me feel like I was crafting something. I don't think it can work for every game, but in my opinion, more of them should spend more time crafting and less time gathering resources/ clicking through menus.

text:
Piles of scrap: Where's the "happy medium" between too much gear and too little gear in a game?

I recently got into the Earth Defense Force series. While it has been a blast (literally and figuratively), one thing that stands out about it is that the inventory of weapons among the four classes is massive. At least in EDF 2025, there are no skill trees or upgrades to speak of, so "levelling up" means getting better weapons. For any given weapon, there are multiple variants with varying stats. However, the general trend is that their stats go up overall as you unlock the later variants. While this initially can be fun as you constantly unlock new weapons, it quickly becomes clear that you're just building what amounts to huge piles of "scrap": Weapons that, due to their inferior stats and a lack of unique perks to make up for those stats, are completely useless at anything but the lowest difficulty levels. There's basically no reason to ever go back to lower- level weapons, so while you may technically have a sizeable selection of weapons, the reality is that you'll have maybe a handful of weapons that are actually good while the rest just take up space in the loadout menu. This dilemma is further aggravated by the game's randomized weapon "levelling" system, as it's entirely possible to unlock higher- tier versions of a given weapon, then unlock the lower- tier versions later on. This dilemma isn't unique to EDF. Especially in action games of this type, it's not unusal to quickly realize that there's a lot of gear you'll never use because it's just not worth it. To be clear, this isn't the same as beginner gear, meme items, or gear meant for a specifc play style. Rather, it's gear that has the unfortunate combination of poor performance and a lack of special perks to make up for those stats. Or, in some cases, it does have an outstanding special perk/really good stats in one specific area, but the perk is either so conditional or the other stats are so bad that it's not worth bothering with. As an aside, I'd also include games that don't have a weapon "selection" per se, but have a large perk tree that lets you customize your one weapon to a fairly large degree. You see the exact same kind of dilemma, except the issue lies in the available upgrades/builds. That brings me to my question: How can games find a "happy medium" between too little build variety and having mountains of useless equipment?
label: game_design

text:
Why do you think folk are more accepting toward English-dubbed voiceovers for video games than other mediums?

In the world of live-action tv/film, you get laughed at if you willingly watch foreign stuff in anything but the original languages of the actors on screen. And with animation, especially Japanese produced stuff, there's forever been the "sub vs dub" debate. But with games... it's only a game here and there where I see people very loudly championing for the original actors and performances. We largely just deem English the universal way to experience characters and worlds even if it's not the native one that the developers maybe first envisioned with it. There's some major contrasts to that, like the Yakuza franchise. But even outside of Japanese, a lot of people play things like the Metro games in English. It's largely about Japanese vs English when it comes to video games just because of the huge volume of games they produce, but nowadays even Korean and Chinese titles are becoming more popular. I mean, all these gacha games that MiHoYo makes like Genshin and ZZZ are natively voiced in Chinese, but I almost only see gameplay clips and people sharing stuff in English. This isn't like a "dubs are bad" discussion I'm trying to make. It's just interesting how typically if you're passionate about media that's foreign when it comes to shows and movies, you probably eventually engage with it much more in it's native language. But with games, even passionate gamers still seem mostly prone to just playing all things in English or whatever language reflects their own. Again, it's not a matter of one being better or being wrong, etc. It's just an observation and something I've wondered.
label: gaming_culture

text:
What Makes A Videogame & Does It Matter?

Following Mixtape’s release recently, I have seen some disagreement regarding it being called a videogame. With how broad the medium is for experiences it’s easy for me to dismiss those viewpoints as silly complaints over something that person is simply not interested in, but I still ended up pondering the question of what makes a game a game. A wide range of opinions can be found in even small groups when it comes to asking people what is required to classify something as a game. Some examples I’ve seen; Visual Novels or dialogue-focused games being seen as comics/mangas/books and not “real” games (Doki Doki Literature Club, Disco Elysium). Anything that isn’t pure gameplay being seen as needless additions that don’t matter because “gameplay is king”. Walking Sims (Firewatch, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, What Remains of Edith Finch) dismissed for being “games where all you do is hold W/Up”. Some games being dismissed for not having “real/traditional gameplay” (Heavy Rain, Telltale’s The Walking Dead, Mixtape). Lack of failstates or challenges to win/overcome. For myself I think the flexibility of what a game can be is precisely what makes the medium so interesting. I can find equal fun in the nostalgic trip of Mixtape’s narrative as I can in the high octane and deep combat system of Ninja Gaiden 2. I just want to have fun and memorable experiences made by passionate teams. When sitting down and thinking about all of this I started asking myself the ultimate question of – Does the argument matter? Does it matter if games do or don’t meet some arbitrary requirement to be seen as part of the medium of videogames? Is there a genuine use of pondering this question and what good do those conversation have other than allowing someone who likes to categorise items be happy that the correct label has been applied to the correct cereal box, so to speak? Or, getting real deep into psychoanalysing myself, am I putting too much stock into a topic I should work harder at just ignoring? At which point maybe I should be posting to r/ mentalhealth haha. Some thoughts from others would be great to hear, thanks.
label: gaming_culture

text:
The diminishing returns in graphics and performance of games today vs games 5-10 years ago genuinely infuriating.

The point of this post is to be a sort of frustrated discussion on the diminishing return in graphical fidelity of games vs the cost of getting them to run at a decently playable state compared to older games which obviously ran better and looked incredible. Just to set standards my system is an RTX 3060 laptop GPU + i7-12650h and 16gb of ddr5 Ram. I'd like to use 6 games in 3 pairs of comparison - Gears 5 vs E-Day, Halo Infinite vs Campaign Evolved and Doom Eternal vs Dark Ages. Gears was the sole reason why i even got so frustrated to write this post. Even if i'm alone on this opinion i would like to share it - I do not, and CAN NOT see any sort of meaningful difference in Gears 5 vs EDay when it comes to graphics. Does the ground look a bit more detailed? sure. Does the lighting look better? can't tell, even in direct side by sides. My system ran Gears 5 at a locked 120fps without upscaling at mostly high to some medium settings. The game looked incredible, ran incredible even in very demanding areas only dropped to barely 100fps? This same system can barely run EDay at 40-50fps on low dlss quality. It's genuinely so annoying, where i even cranked my settings to high in E-Dday just to see the differences in my own damn screenshots and the difference is so meaningless that it really does not warrant the absolute downgrade in playability and performance. Hell, i spent 20 minutes seeing 3 different graphical comparison videos and came to the same conclusion - Why is there a need for extremely subtle graphical upgrades which practically no one is going to look at, nor care about being catered to so much? Every game needs to have x polygons per object when having half of x just does the job well and is not taxing on the system? My same point of comparison applies to Halo, where campaign evolved sure looks good but practically it really is not much improved my Halo Infinite, where many times Infinite actually looked better and ran better. And my last point of contention was DOOM where i seriously cannot understand the decisions many studios and companies make - Why is DOOM of all things a game where you must focus on graphics and literally alienate so much of your playerbase by having such high system requirements? 8GB Vram minimum to get your game running, which sure is standard but for what? so that you can have mandatory ray tracing in your game to avoid traditional baked lights? On a side by side comparison DOOM TDA definitely is much more graphically impressive than Eternal, but WHO CARES? Who actually plays Doom for it's graphical detail when not a single person is gonna look at the god damn assets during it's hyper fast motion? Doom eternal looked so good, ran so good without having useless focus on graphical fidelity and real time ray tracing. My post can also include examples like Arkham Knight, Uncharted 4, Spiderman 2018 etc and directly comparing them to how their successors and sequels play such as Gotham Knights, Spiderman 2 etc and how bad their performance is compared to the minimal visual upgrade and focus on unnecessary things. Why is the industry headed this way man?

text:
Coming to grips with the fact that some games and/or genres are simply "too hard" for me now.

So I hate to say but I'm pushing 40 and I've noticed my preference for gaming continues to evolve and change. One thing I've noticed, even 10 years ago, was that my reflexes in FPS games weren't as sharp as they used to be, so I've basically stopped playing any FPS's especially in multiplayer. I'm just not as good anymore and can't compete with people who have more time and sharper reflexes than me. I'm okay with this, and to be honest I feel like FPS's haven't really evolved much over the past 10-15 years, so it's simply a genre I don't play anymore. There are, however, several games that I really REALLY wanted to beat and that I put a lot of time into but simply had to put down because I could not for the life of me beat them. To cut to the chase, in the 2010's I became a Souls fan, starting with Dark Souls 1, then Demon Souls, then Bloodborne, Dark Souls 3, then 2. I have beaten all of these games. Did I use NPC or player summons sometimes to get through a tough boss. Of course I did, and I felt no guilt about it. It was in the game to be used, maybe as a crutch, but I never felt like it was cheating. Then Sekiro comes out, and everything changed. I struggled to get through that game. It was brutal. Some of the bosses were utter brick walls for me, but I would always, just barely, overcome them. Any souls fan will know the wave of relief you feel once you beat a super hard boss you're stuck on. That all came to an end when I hit the final boss, Isshin, the Sword Saint. I tried maybe 20 times and couldn't even come CLOSE to beating him. I didn't even feel like I was making progress at all. If anything I was getting worse as I went. I know 20 times maybe even isn't a lot to some people, but in the back of my mind, I knew I simply wasn't having fun anymore. Sure I could've spent hours and hours putting in dozens more attempts. I would probably beat it eventually. But it was the first time I nope'd out hard. I decided I would never beat Sekiro, and had no desire to ever play it again. Shame. This happened a few more times over the years (you'll notice it's in roughly the same genre). Elden Ring I was somehow able to beat, especially with the Mimic Tear and player summons, but the DLC final boss, once again, was a brick wall. I did what I did with Sekiro and set it down and vowed never to touch it again. Hollow Knight was so great, but then Silksong came out... I loved it at first, and struggled to get through the first Act. Got to the second Act and hit another brick wall. A 15 wave fight of enemies. I tried dozens of times, realized I was just pissed off and not having any fun, and set it down for good. I'm not sure I'll ever beat it, which is a shame because the game was pretty excellent otherwise. Since these experiences, I've had another shift in genre preference. I decided I'm pretty much done with the Souls/Souls-like genre, or any sort of "ultra hard" action game. I've been getting back into JRPG's and tactical RPG's, since even though they can be challenging, it's less about your sharp reflexes and more about thinking and strategy which currently I prefer. Anyone else experience this? I'm kind of sad that, due to age and creeping difficulty, I've been pushed out of genres I used to love. It's okay I guess, since there's other genres I still enjoy. I'll probably buy the next FromSoft game (not Duskbloods) but I'm worried I won't be able to beat it. It's a shame but I guess I just have to move on.

Anyone else getting more sensitive to stutter and bad frame pacing as they get older?

So yeah, I’m 40 now and I’ve noticed something kinda annoying. When I was younger I could play literally anything — 30 FPS, stutter, janky camera movement, whatever — and it never bothered me. No idea if it’s the engine, frametime spikes, animations running at different framerates… I just know I feel it. I also have pretty bad eyesight (strong myopia, one eye weaker, no 3D vision), so maybe my brain used to compensate better and now it doesn’t. Just wondering if anyone around my age has the same thing. Like, becoming way more sensitive to motion issues in games? Funny thing is, I always thought getting older meant I’d need less visual quality… but nope. I don’t really “see” the benefit of 4K or super high FPS anymore, but if the motion isn’t perfect I feel like crap. Getting old is wild.

text:
Respecting the player's time and how Marvel's Spider-Man on PS4 shattered that rule

I think the biggest win of "respecting a player's time" versus player immersion and enjoyment of the game as presented is that Insomniac's Spider-Man on PS4 has fast-travel and has a specific trophy for using it 5 times. That number is important, because according to data tracked on psnprofiles.com, 66.43% of players got the trophy for PSNprofiles users, and 38% got it overall among Playstation players. Like, how many times do you fast-travel in a typical open-world game with fast-travel? The answer is definitely a lot. I bet most players who played Skyrim probably fast-traveled more than five times before they finished the Bleak Falls Barrow quest for Whiterun. So let's focus on that 66.43%/38% of the players who got that trophy, and compare it to other trophies that were nearly at or at a higher percentage of completion that players of the game received for completely optional content or end-game content. 66.41%/35.2% of players got the optional "Backpacker" Trophy for finding all of the hidden backpacks. 65.77%/35.8% of players got the optional "Hero for Higher" Trophy for getting to the very top of the Avengers tower and perching there for a second. 75.47%/47.8% of players got the optional "Amazing Coverage" Trophy for activating every single Surveillance Tower. But more importantly... 83.05%/65.4% of players completed Act 1 76.75%/56.0% of players completed Act 2 71.91%/47.9% of players completed Act 3 That third one is especially telling for one reason: That is the number of players who went through the entire game's campaign, which takes around 17 hours per How Long to Beat and means that more people did that than used the fast travel system more than four times from beginning to end. That is a staggering number to look at when you think about it. Once you unlock the ability to fast travel in the game after completing the mission "Wheels within Wheels", you can pretty much fast travel at any point from then on by clicking a point of interest from the menu map. If you don't like the subway animations, you can even disable them to make the fast travel faster. Yet a statistically significant enough amount of people chose to beat the entire game instead of fast-travelling five times during their entire run. I'll admit, I'm one of them. Why would I fast travel for three seconds to get to a mission all the way across the map like 2km+ away when that's 2km+ of New York skylines to swing through and have a blast for five minutes while I catch up with the audio banter and maybe stop a few crimes along the way? Fast-Travel would have been a complete waste of the game's potential and the enjoyment of the traversal. I still think that's an amazing statistic to consider. More people beat the entire game than fast-traveled.

text:
The term "remake" is too broad of an umbrella and we should tighten it's definition

Recently i've been thinking thanks to the various "remakes" and the discourse around them, that the word remake is used way too broadly. What i mean by this is that games are marketed and discussed as remakes when in reality some of them call themselves reimaginings. Why do i think this? Well firstly i would like to present to you my taxonomy on the various ways you'll see a game preserved. I will also be using music analogies here to make my point better (Not sure how useful these will be but oh well) Port: This is the most basic. You put the game on PC as is with no changes. Emulation also technically falls under this. Game collections usually fall under this. Basically like putting the song on another album or even reprinting the album Expanded Port: This is where you take the already existing game and just add more content to it or even some tiny QoLs. This includes stuff like fighting game revisions. Basically an Extended version of the song Remaster: Now you take the assets of the original game and just... Upscale them to modern standards. Not changing them, no. Just upscaling. In music terms from Wikipedia: Remastering is the process of making a new master for an album, film, or any other creation. Basically you're making a new master for the game but you're not changing much about it Remake: The game is now faithfully rebuilt from the ground up with brand new graphics, presentation, minor QoLs, and you can also remix the soundtrack now. Games like Spyro Reignited Trilogy and Crash Bandicoot N'Sane Trilogy fall under this category in my opinion regardless of what the Steam page says. In music terms it's like a new band performing the original song faithfully. The instruments and performers are different but they're still playing the same composition and arrangement Reimagining: THIS is the real category that most "remakes" fall into. You take the core premise of the game like the setting, story, characters HOWEVER now you are changing the core gameplay in big ways, making dialogue changes, forcing QoLs on people, changing progression etc. This includes "remakes" like Yakuza Kiwami 1,2,3, Trails in the Sky the 1st and 2nd, Persona 3 Reload and Persona 4 Revival. Almost like remixing a song. The core is there but you can't call the song a rerecording cause it changes too much compared to the original This however brings us to another problem... When a reimagining pretending to be a remake comes out a definitive version of a game stops existing cause now you not only have the original game there as the authentic experience. You now have this reimagined version made for modern audiences specifically to get them in the game. So my question is: Which version of the game do i play? Cause one is the original while the other is a remix of the game rather than a remake. Which brings me to my point that we're using the term "remake" wrong and it's too broad. Keep in mind i'm not saying that these reimaginings are bad in fact they are nice to have but we really need to tighten up the definitions at last Examples of developers describing their "remakes" as reimaginings taken directly from their Steam pages Trails in the Sky the 1st: This stunning, award-nominated remake reimagines the beloved classic with new breathtaking visuals, refined gameplay, and the first unforgettable adventure across Liberl Kingdom. ("Remake reimagines" is literally a contradiction) Persona 3 Reload: Persona 3 Reload is a captivating reimagining of the genre-defining RPG, reborn for the modern era. Then in the Key Features. Experience the pivotal game of the Persona series faithfully remade with cutting-edge graphics, modernized quality-of-life features, and signature stylish UI.(Like what is this? Pick a lane ATLUS. Is this a faithful remake or a reimagining?) Resident Evil 4 Remake: Featuring modernized gameplay, a reimagined storyline, and vividly detailed graphics, Resident Evil 4 marks the rebirth of an industry juggernaut. (Notice how not only does it calls it's story "reimagined" but the game describes itself as a REBIRTH)

text:
Why are there so few RPGs based on real historical events?

Ever since I played KCD I have been thinking about this. RPGs as a genre seem like the perfect fit for telling real stories, you've got character progression, faction systems, branching narratives, resource management, like why wouldn’t we have more RPGs set in the Roman Empire or Medieval Britain for example. Period historic ones, I mean. When you look at RPGs overall it's like 85% fantasy, 10% sci-fi, and then KCD and KCD 2 standing almost completely alone, or that is my unlearned impression. I mention KCD specifically because it pretty much proved how the low (actually zero) fantasy setting can still work and the sequel was just as good and delivered despite the hype, and the historical accuracy is one of the crucial points of the game.. The Bohemian setting doesn’t just add flavor, it turned out to be the whole selling point because it made every quest feel like it mattered in a way that a random fantasy quest never can, with villages and nooks and rivurlets that would look “generic” in other games being all important landmarks, and all seeped in history and culture of the boiling pot that was Central Europe in the 15th century because when you hear about something that really actually happened it's always going to feel more real than fantasy. But I think the problem is in how RPGs have always handled player agency. The whole appeal of the genre is that your choices shape the world, and history (by definition, in a history centered RPG) has already been shaped. You can't let the player assassinate Julius Caesar in 50 BC and then have Cleopatra's storyline play out normally, your character can’t change grand events (while still being “historical”) although it does provide a lot in the way of character building, especially minor characters. Warhorse solved this by making you a bit of a nobody, Henry's story exists in the margins of history, below the level where your choices would contradict the record but that's a pretty narrow design space and I suspect most studios look at something like that and conclude it’s easier to just make an original fantasy setting. There is an upcoming RPG I discovered though that deals with real world events, Hollow Home, one of those Disco Elysium like games (a purely narrative based RPG with no combat and a lot of dialogue) based on true events that happened (/are happening?) during the Russo-Ukraine war It has me curious about because these types of games are purely narrative focused so the setting is not just going to be there for flavor or aesthetics, or I hope not considering the bleak and frankly depressing subject matter, so I assume they’re betting on that gut weight based in a grounded, somewhat bleak story that fantasy only seldom achieves (since it’s based on the events of a real ongoing war, this one is bound to stir up some emotions one way or another, that’s for sure) By the by, I think another problem is also meticulously researching the specific history of any single setting and then choosing how to portray it as a work of art (which parts, what to transform or change…because it can never be “real” history, no more than a book), and it’s massively underestimated one at that. Because a fantasy RPG with shoddy worldbuilding will get called generic or bland at worst, but a historical RPG that botches the history will get absolutely ridiculed by the internet, actual historians writing massive takedowns of your armor designs in the comments (which is half the entertainment value of some YouTube channels but probably not ideal if its your baby they’re pulling apart) That way, the accuracy bar ends up way higher while the creative freedom shrinks, and most studios probably just don't think that’s worth it, unless the real story they want to tell actually matters to them a lot, then they might still risk it. Otherwise, I think it’s simple that it’s safer to work and let your creative freedome loose in a fantasy setting, rather than unknowingly stirring some hornet nest because you didn’t handle a specific historical portrayal with care. What’s your take on this, if you have one?

text:
Does violence enhance GTA V's satire, or undermine it?

So I've been replaying GTA V in preparation for VI coming soon, and was struck by the torture sequence where Trevor interrogates Mr K after you kidnap him from the rival intelligence agency. I remember feeling uncomfortable with this sequence when I first played the game, but that reaction has definitely increased in the intervening years. Back when I first played it I mostly remember it feeling edgy and excessive in the way GTA often does, if a little "too far". But replaying it now, what struck me was how tonally jarring it is to have something so brutal turned into essentially a series of minigames / quicktime prompts with achievements linked to keeping your victim from passing out. I rewatched American Psycho recently too and my reaction to GTA V quite reminds me of my reaction when I first read that novel. Both of these works made me feel queasy (an understatement: I'd quite like to permanently remove the memory of some passages from AP from my brain), but in very different ways. American Psycho is obviously horrific at points, and disturbing because you're trapped inside Bateman’s first-person perspective, but there's still an element of objective distance in reading. GTA V feels different because instead of observing the violence, you're actively performing it. There's a lot of other parallels and in a sense both are doing the same essential thing: satirising late capitalism, consumerism, superficiality, violence as spectacle, etc. Both depict worlds where nothing seems to have depth or lasting consequence and where hyperconsumption and extreme violence exist as part of the same system and reflect back on each other. But the medium, to me, makes a huge difference. American Psycho implicates the reader, but you're still ultimately a passive observer held at a distance and so able to make a moral judgement as you read. GTA V collapses that distance entirely by making the violence entertaining and interactive. But what I genuinely can’t decide is whether that makes GTA V’s satire more effective or less effective. I know games like Hotline Miami very explicitly ask you to reflect on the violence and your own enjoyment of it, but is this what GTA V is doing too, with the added, AP-style layer of consumption as a juxtaposition? Does your participation deepen the critique because it takes the extremity to a new level, and in its endless repetition allow you to experience its emptiness firsthand? Or does making violence into a fun gameplay loop basically undermine the point? Curious what other people think.

text:
Cyberpunk 2077 Dialogue - Beautiful Stylized Writing or a Cringey Mess?

I'm playing through the game for the first time and can't help but think the dialogue is super cringey. It's stilted and tries too hard to be cool. I'm sure I'm not the first person to share the opinion here, but... this ain't preem in the game biz. Most conversations play out as if the characters are limited in how many words they're allowed to say. For example, "Need'ta ask a question" vs, "I need to ask you a question." I noticed this early on and now I can't stop seeing it in the writing because it occurs literally in every conversation. I get this is drawn heavily from Neuromancer, but many of the lines are delivered as though the voice actor had little to no coaching on tone, emphasis, or the context of the scene. Dexter DeShawn's lines are a good example of this. Combine the truncated sentence structure with voice acting that lacked a little conviction and you get conversations that feel like people are reading a foreign language. I have no issue with the use of novel slang from this world, but I think it was done poorly here. I could totally buy into it being colloquial sentence structure and slang, but it's really inconsistent and not delivered in a way that is believable. That's why it's jarring to me. Abbreviated sentence structure as a way of communicating happens like once per conversation, but it's never the WHOLE conversation. The dialogue FEELS like a team of Polish writers with no true understanding of US urban culture put together a 'cool guy' script in a foreign language then a separate team translated it after. I believe you could give the same game to Rockstar and their dialogue could feature all of the same slang but be delivered in a way that felt authentic and genuinely cool. None of this is a dealbreaker for me, but it's quite disappointing to see it from a studio with this much experience and funding. I'm having fun with the core gameplay loop overall and bought the DLC to extend the adventure, but I wouldn't be able to power through for the story alone if the gunplay and tech weren't so satisfying. Anyone else feel something similar? Video version of the discussion here.

text:
How do you deal with certain recurring themes in dark fiction?

Content warning: This post discusses sexual violence, rape, reproductive coercion, forced pregnancy, forced marriage, and loss of bodily autonomy. I have been struggling with something in games lately, and I genuinely want to hear how other people deal with it. I love dark fantasy, horror, dystopian fiction and generally very dark games. Violence, death, body horror, oppressive governments, war and horrible fictional societies do not normally bother me much. But I have become increasingly exhausted by how often sexual violence and the loss of women's bodily autonomy appear in these settings. Rape, forced pregnancy, reproductive coercion, forced marriage, women being treated as breeding stock, women being valued because they can produce children, etc. It feels like I keep encountering some variation of it whenever a fictional world wants to demonstrate how horrible or dystopian it is. Gears of War is what set me off today. I have loved Gears since I was younger and was having a great time replaying the first game. Then I started reading more of the lore surrounding the Fortification Act and the Birthing Crèches, and it genuinely soured my mood enough that I turned the game off. But this is not really a complaint specifically about Gears. Gears was just the thing that pushed me over the edge today. I also want to make something very clear: I am NOT saying these subjects should never appear in fiction. They happen in reality. They can be important subjects to explore. They can be extremely effective world-building. I understand why dystopian fiction deals with bodily autonomy and why sexual violence can be used to explore power and oppression. My problem is how incredibly often it seems to happen. Eventually I find myself thinking: can we have one horrible dystopian society where the writers find some other way of demonstrating that it is horrible without eventually taking away women's sexual or reproductive autonomy? It particularly bothers me because the biological inequality already frustrates me. Women are the ones who physically experience pregnancy and childbirth, and then so much fiction takes that biological reality and turns it into another opportunity for somebody else to claim ownership over their bodies. It makes me angry in a way that fictional violence normally does not. And I know these characters are not real. Nobody is actually being harmed by the fictional events on my screen. I understand the difference between depicting something and endorsing it. That does not stop the emotional reaction. So I am genuinely asking other people who enjoy dark games, books, fantasy, horror, science fiction, etc.: If sexual violence or reproductive coercion is something that particularly bothers you, how do you deal with encountering it so often? Do you compartmentalise it from the rest of the story? Avoid learning more about that part of the lore? Take a break and come back? Avoid certain games entirely? Has repeated exposure to the trope made you more frustrated with it over time? I do not want to stop enjoying dark fiction. I just wish this particular form of darkness did not feel so ubiquitous, and right now I am struggling to stop it from souring things I otherwise love.

text:
Players say they want NPCs with their own lives, but I think watching is as far is it goes

Just to be upfront: I work in player research in the games industry. No product, no links, just an idea I want to discuss. Here's my claim: what players actually value in living worlds is spectating and not cohabiting. If NPCs genuinely lived their own lives, most players would stop engaging with them within the first session. Here's why I think that. Twenty years of autonomous NPC attempts produce the same two reactions: noticed behaviour becomes an anecdote we retell for years, and missing behaviour makes us call the world empty. Both are about being in the audience, neither requires actual interaction. Then when researchers recently dropped hundreds of AI agents into sandbox worlds and these agents formed jobs and even a religion, everyone read the articles, but nobody asked to be a part of it. There's a darker version too, where an NPC with real agency competes with you for authorship. A world that changes on its own is atmospheric until it builds something where you were going to build. The best counterargument I can think of is that nobody has shipped real cohabitation, so players never had the chance to want it. Maybe the watching preference is just learned from decades of NPCs not being worth talking to. That's the idea. I'd rather be wrong, so if your experience contradicts it, I'm listening.

text:
Harder difficulty should not mean less health

[EDIT: I intended this to be read as any adjustment to health/damage, be it to the player or to enemies] It was introduced as a way to get round performance limitations and it should be retired. In Doom (1993), harder difficulty just meant more enemies. The enemies behaved the same and did the same damage, there were just more of them [Nightmare mode excepted]. Playing on Ultraviolence was a huge adrenaline rush from start to finish. Within a few years, that way of increasing difficulty had died out. But why? It was the move to true 3D that did it. The first few years of true 3D games had tougher enemies and less of them, because the computers couldn't handle displaying as many entities as in the pseudo-3D Doom days. Good examples of this include the difference between Blood and Blood 2: the first game was frantic with enemies, and the sequel (by now true 3D) was much slower with sparser enemies. The first Unreal is another example: bullet-sponge enemies and never more than three at a time. Now, we have computers that think nothing of displaying thirty full-3D on-screen enemies at 120fps, so why does increasing the difficulty still make fundamental changes to how the game is balanced, instead of just giving us more things to fight? I expect that it's because changing the number of enemies is more work than simply tweaking damage levels, but as a proportion of work put into a game it's surely a drop in the ocean. Are there any other reasons why we've never gone back to the old style of increasing difficulty?

text:
The modern definition of accessibility is having a negative impact on games

I’ve noticed that accessibility has recently morphed into something new. What was once some extra game options to assist the disabled (e.g. colorblind) has become a much more wholistic approach to game design meant to make a game accessible to as many people as possible. This seems to be motivated by some combination of extreme egalitarianism and a desire to sell as many units of product as possible. I’ve participated in several healthy debates here on this very forum on this topic in recent months. People throw around examples of fighting games providing “modern controls” or Civ7 eliminating core series mechanics in a desire to reduce complex micromanagement of units. Others make an analogy to soccer and the reducto ad absurdum of allowing players to use their hands in an effort to make the game more accessible - and also making it less like actual soccer. All of these are interesting topics. But what made me post this is the recent release and review of Wolverine. This whole topic seems to have broken containment and is now being talked about everywhere. SkillUp himself opens his review with the observation that Wolverine appears to have been designed assuming the player is very dumb. And he points to this new definition of accessibility (not the original concept) as a big problem. Then this morning I came across a Reddit thread where someone had gone through all of the Insomnic leaks and watched the zoom calls that were going on through development. https://www.reddit.com/r/GamingLeaksAndRumours/comments/1vplboa/marvels_wolverine_almost_had_a_crossbow_adaptive/ It’s fascinating to see the curtain pulled back. Early versions of Wolverine had a very novel combat system where the DuelSense left and right triggers activated Wolverines left and right hands with different attacks based on the trigger pressure. The whole thing was scrapped because accessibility controllers only have trigger buttons, not pressure sensitive controls. What we were left with was the universally panned “press square 3 to 5 times and activate and animation system that is by all accounts extremely boring. This accessibility first design seems to have influenced more than just combat with the scent lines, gps navigators, and white paint everywhere. I cannot think of a more clear example of how we all lose as a result of this modern approach to game design. For traditional accessibility system to even matter, the game needs to be good first. It’s interesting that this whole topic has gone mainstream as a result of Wolverine. I suspect the game is being scapegoated to some extent and that this sentiment has been building for a while. Do you think there will be a course correction from the industry? I don’t think it’s guaranteed. Game developers can be quite intransigent when the issue is important to them. As an aside - I find the white paint thing funny. People have been making fun of yellow paint for a while now. I am almost certain that Wolverine originally had yellow paint. Someone must have e pointed out that yellow paint has a bad reputation so someone had the bright idea to make it white paint. Take that to the bank.

text:
Lockpicking - Something I did not expect about Gothic Remake

Up until recently my feelings about lockpicking/hacking minigames in RPG games have been lukewarm at best. Gothic Remake changed that. I was very hyped about Gothic Remake because the og game played a pivotal role in my adolescence. When I finally got my hands on it, I was pretty ecstatic, except for a specific system - lockpicking. It was changed dramatically. From this simple "press left-right buttons randomly in a sequence" system to a demanding puzzle involving tumblers and plates. Picking a lock in the original game took few seconds at most, whereas in the remake that's very rare, some locks can take 10+ minutes to solve, assuming you do solve them. At first I resented this change greatly. However after playing a while, I realized that this might be the best lockpicking system I have ever seen in a RPG game. I understand this statement may be too strong, but let me elaborate before commenting. Lockpicking is pretty much always an optional, horizontal progression system which allows the player to invest their effort or progression into getting more loot. It's basically adding more content to the game, slowing down the player in an immersive and inobtrusive way. It's a good way to make the world more interactive, to give the player an opportunity to earn extra loot, to add more gameplay into a game. It has become quite an RPG staple at this point. The problem is that in most cases you will find a lock solving strategy and then every lock will be the same. Lockpicking in Gothic remake is unique because while there are several strategies, you never know which one will work before actually trying them out, and many locks are seemingly designed to punish specific strategies. It forces you to actually engage with the minigame instead of doing the same thing over and over. It means that while the average time to pick a lock might be 20s, specific locks can take 10+ minutes to solve, assuming you do solve them. Another interesting thing about Gothic Remake's lockpicking is the implementation. While most RPGs sprinkle locked chests fairly evenly across the game (e.g. random locked chests in wilderness, dungeons etc.), in Gothic most locked objects are far more clustered. While there are chests in dungeons and such, they are mostly unlocked, whereas populated areas (e.g. major hubs) have a ton of them. Lockpicking can take time, and takes place in real time (unlike say Skyrim), and since NPCs have schedules and reactive behavior, this also plays a huge role in what you can unlock. Some houses just have someone nearby all the time and you effectively can't lockpick chests inside them unless you start murdering people. Sometimes people walk on you while lockpicking just because it started raining and their routine made them hide in a house during the day. Locked chest in a dungeon is in a way just waste of player's time. But it's completely different in a city because it integrates so well into the rest of the game. The whole package creates an interesting, dynamic experience. There's a ton of players, both new and veterans, who hate it because it's so demanding (and loot isn't that interesting). Plenty of people have tried to make or use various calculators and "lock solvers" which remove most of the challenge. But I don't see a point of that because the system is still very optional and you won't be missing on anything substantial if you choose to not interact with lockpicking at all. The idea of "I just can't open this" is also not something that frustrates me, but adds to the experience. But for me it's one of the strongest aspects of Gothic Remake, one that I did not expect at all. I spent about 8 hours cleaning out every house in Old, New and Swamp camp yesterday, completely ignoring the rest of the game, and I had a blast.
